title: Lesson 5: Choosing the Right Method
text:
The Decision Framework
Choosing between PLS, CCA, regression, and related methods depends on answering a few key questions about your data and research goals.

title: Lesson 5: Choosing the Right Method
text:
Key Questions to Ask

Question 1: What is Your Research Goal?
The first and most important question divides methods into two camps:















TipRule of Thumb



If you care more about predicting new cases accurately, lean toward regression methods. If you care more about understanding relationships, lean toward PLS or CCA.




Question 2: What is Your Sample Size vs. Variable Count?
This is often the deciding factor between methods:











Question 3: Do You Have Distinct X and Y Blocks?
Some methods require a clear distinction between predictors (X) and outcomes (Y):



Scenario
Method Options




Clear X → Y relationship
PLS-R, regression, PCR


Symmetric exploration (no clear direction)
PLS-C, CCA


Single block of variables
PCA, factor analysis


Multiple blocks (>2)
Multi-block PLS, GCCA

title: Lesson 5: Choosing the Right Method
text:
Practical Scenarios
Let’s walk through common research scenarios and the recommended methods.

Scenario 1: Brain-Behavior with Few Subjects
Situation: 50 subjects, 100 brain regions, 5 behavior scores


Subjects (n): 50 


Brain variables (p): 100 


Behavior variables (q): 5 


p/n ratio: 2 


Since p > n, CCA would overfit.


RECOMMENDED: PLS


Why PLS?

Variables exceed samples (p > n)
CCA would produce spuriously high correlations
PLS finds stable patterns despite high dimensionality



Scenario 2: Predicting Clinical Outcomes
Situation: 500 patients, 20 biomarkers, predict treatment response (single outcome)


Patients (n): 500 


Biomarkers (p): 20 


Outcome: single variable (treatment response)


p/n ratio: 0.04 


Since n >> p and goal is prediction:


RECOMMENDED: Multiple regression or PLS-R



If biomarkers are correlated: PLS-R


If biomarkers are independent: Multiple regression




Scenario 3: Genetics and Neuroimaging
Situation: 200 subjects, 10,000 SNPs, 50 brain measures


Subjects (n): 200 


SNPs (p): 10000 


Brain measures (q): 50 


Total variables: 10050 


Extremely high-dimensional!


RECOMMENDED: Sparse PLS or penalized methods



Standard PLS would work but sparse PLS


would identify key SNPs more clearly.




Scenario 4: Comparing Two Questionnaires
Situation: 300 participants, two 10-item questionnaires, want to understand shared structure


Participants (n): 300 


Questionnaire A items (p): 10 


Questionnaire B items (q): 10 


Total variables: 20 


n / total variables: 15 


Adequate sample size, symmetric exploration.


RECOMMENDED: CCA or PLS-C



Both would work well. CCA if you want


maximum correlation, PLS-C if covariance.

title: Lesson 5: Choosing the Right Method
text:
Quick Reference Guide

When to Use PLS
Choose PLS when:

More variables than samples (p > n)
Multicollinearity is present
You want to explore covariance structure
Robust patterns more important than optimal fit
Sample size is limited



When to Use CCA
Choose CCA when:

Many more samples than variables (n >> p)
You want maximum correlation
Statistical significance testing is important
No clear predictor/outcome distinction
Both variable sets are similar in size



When to Use Regression
Choose standard regression when:

Clear single outcome variable
Predictors are largely independent
Good sample size relative to predictors
Prediction accuracy is the goal



When to Use PCR
Choose PCR when:

Multicollinearity in predictors
Want to reduce dimensionality first
Single outcome to predict
Variance in X is informative

title: Lesson 5: Choosing the Right Method
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Using CCA with High-Dimensional Data


Code
# DON'T do this:
# n = 100 subjects, p = 500 brain regions, q = 20 behaviors
# CCA will find perfect correlations that don't generalize

# DO this instead:
# Use PLS, which handles p > n naturally




Mistake 2: Ignoring Multicollinearity


Code
# If your predictors are correlated:
set.seed(42)
n <- 100
x1 <- rnorm(n)
x2 <- x1 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)  # Highly correlated with x1
x3 <- x1 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)  # Also correlated

# Check correlation
cor_matrix <- cor(cbind(x1, x2, x3))
print(round(cor_matrix, 2))


     x1   x2   x3
x1 1.00 0.97 0.96
x2 0.97 1.00 0.93
x3 0.96 0.93 1.00


With correlations this high, standard regression will have unstable coefficients. Use PLS, PCR, or Ridge regression instead.


Mistake 3: Choosing Based on Name Recognition
Just because you’ve heard of a method doesn’t mean it’s right for your data:

“Everyone uses regression” → But is your data suited for it?
“PLS is too complicated” → It’s actually quite intuitive
“CCA is more rigorous” → Not if your sample size is small

Choose based on data characteristics, not familiarity.

title: Lesson 5: Choosing the Right Method
text:
Decision Flowchart Summary
Here’s a simplified decision process:

Is your goal prediction or pattern discovery?

Prediction → Consider regression family
Pattern discovery → Consider PLS or CCA

Do you have more variables than samples?

Yes → Use PLS (not CCA or standard regression)
No → Continue to next question

Are your X variables correlated (multicollinear)?

Yes → Use PLS, PCR, or Ridge
No → Standard regression may work

Do you need formal statistical tests?

Yes → CCA has established tests, PLS uses permutation
No → Either works

Do you have a clear X → Y direction?

Yes → PLS-R or regression
No → PLS-C or CCA

title: Lesson 5: Choosing the Right Method
text:
Exercises

Exercise 1: Scenario Analysis
For each scenario, decide which method you would use and explain why:

80 subjects, 200 genes, 5 disease markers
1000 subjects, 10 demographics, predicting income
150 subjects, 30 personality items, 30 cognitive scores



Exercise 2: Sample Size Planning
If you want to use CCA and have 50 variables in each block (X and Y), approximately how many subjects do you need?


Code
# Rule of thumb for CCA: n should be at least 10-20 times total variables
total_vars <- 50 + 50
min_n_conservative <- 20 * total_vars
min_n_liberal <- 10 * total_vars

cat("Conservative estimate:", min_n_conservative, "subjects\n")


Conservative estimate: 2000 subjects


Code
cat("Liberal estimate:", min_n_liberal, "subjects\n")


Liberal estimate: 1000 subjects


Code
cat("\nIf you have fewer subjects, consider PLS instead.\n")



If you have fewer subjects, consider PLS instead.




Exercise 3: Method Switching
You initially used CCA but found very high correlations (r > 0.95) between latent variables. Your sample size is 80 and you have 60 variables total.
What might be happening? What should you do?






NoteAnswer





With n = 80 and p = 60, you’re in the danger zone for CCA. The high correlations are likely spurious due to overfitting.
Solution: Switch to PLS, which will give you more realistic (and generalizable) covariance estimates. You should also use cross-validation to assess how well your patterns replicate.

title: Lesson 5: Choosing the Right Method
text:
Summary

Key Takeaways

Sample size relative to variables is often the deciding factor
PLS is more robust when data is limited or variables are correlated
CCA is preferred when you have abundant data and want maximum correlation
Research goals matter: prediction vs. pattern discovery
No method is universally best - match the method to your data



Final Checklist
Before running your analysis, verify:

I know my n (samples) and p (variables) ratio
I’ve checked for multicollinearity
I’ve defined my research goal (predict vs. explore)
I’ve identified which set is X and which is Y (if applicable)
I’ve chosen a method that matches my data characteristics
I have a plan for validation (permutation, cross-validation, etc.)

title: Lesson 3: Types of PLS Methods
text:
The PLS Family Tree
PLS isn’t one method - it’s a family of related techniques. The key differences are:

What matrix is decomposed (covariance vs correlation)
What the second dataset contains (behaviors, tasks, groups)
Whether prediction or pattern-finding is the goal



Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
set.seed(42)

title: Lesson 3: Types of PLS Methods
text:
PLS Regression (PLS-R)

The Prediction Goal
PLS Regression was developed in chemometrics for prediction. The goal is to predict Y from X.
Key characteristics:

Iterative algorithm (NIPALS)
Extracts components from X that best predict Y
Can handle more predictors than observations
Output includes regression coefficients



How PLS-R Works











Mathematical Formulation
PLS-R iteratively finds:

Weight vectors w that maximize cov(Xw, Y)
Scores t = Xw
Loadings p that relate t back to X
Regression of Y on t

Then deflates X and repeats for more components.


Code
# Simplified PLS-R demonstration (1 component)
n <- 50; p <- 10
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
Y <- X[, 1] + 0.5 * X[, 2] + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)  # Y depends on X1, X2

# Center
X_c <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
Y_c <- scale(Y, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)

# NIPALS algorithm (simplified, 1 iteration)
# Initialize
w <- t(X_c) %*% Y_c
w <- w / sqrt(sum(w^2))  # Normalize

# Compute scores
t_scores <- X_c %*% w

# Compute loadings
p_load <- t(X_c) %*% t_scores / sum(t_scores^2)

# Regression coefficient for Y
c_coef <- sum(Y_c * t_scores) / sum(t_scores^2)

cat("PLS-R Results (1 component):\n")


PLS-R Results (1 component):


Code
cat("Weights (w) - showing top 3 predictors:\n")


Weights (w) - showing top 3 predictors:


Code
top3 <- order(abs(w), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
for (i in top3) {
  cat(sprintf("  X%d: %.3f\n", i, w[i]))
}


  X1: 0.933
  X9: 0.226
  X4: 0.156


Code
cat("\nR² with 1 component:", round(cor(t_scores * c_coef, Y_c)^2, 3), "\n")



R² with 1 component: 0.69 




When to Use PLS-R






NoteUse PLS-R When:




Your goal is prediction
You have more predictors than observations (p > n)
You want regression coefficients
You’re coming from a chemometrics/machine learning context

title: Lesson 3: Types of PLS Methods
text:
PLS Correlation (PLS-C)

The Pattern-Finding Goal
PLS Correlation (often just called “PLS” in neuroimaging) focuses on finding symmetric patterns between two variable sets.
Key characteristics:

Single SVD operation
Treats X and Y symmetrically
Finds patterns that maximally covary
No prediction coefficients



How PLS-C Works











Mathematical Formulation
PLS-C performs SVD on the cross-covariance (or cross-correlation) matrix:
\[R = X^T Y \quad \text{(or standardized)}\] \[R = U S V^T\]
Then computes scores:

Brain scores: \(X \cdot U\)
Behavior scores: \(Y \cdot V\)



Code
# PLS-C demonstration
n <- 50; p1 <- 10; p2 <- 5
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p1), n, p1)
Y <- matrix(rnorm(n * p2), n, p2)

# Create relationship
latent <- rnorm(n)
X[, 1:3] <- X[, 1:3] + outer(latent, c(0.8, 0.5, 0.3))
Y[, 1:2] <- Y[, 1:2] + outer(latent, c(0.7, 0.4))

# Center
X_c <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
Y_c <- scale(Y, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)

# Cross-covariance
R <- t(X_c) %*% Y_c / (n - 1)

# SVD
svd_r <- svd(R)

cat("PLS-C Results:\n")


PLS-C Results:


Code
cat("Singular values:", round(svd_r$d, 3), "\n")


Singular values: 1.368 0.58 0.479 0.322 0.32 


Code
cat("Variance explained:", round((svd_r$d^2)/sum(svd_r$d^2)*100, 1), "%\n")


Variance explained: 70.8 12.7 8.7 3.9 3.9 %




When to Use PLS-C






NoteUse PLS-C When:




Your goal is understanding relationships
Both variable sets are equally important
You want to know which variables on both sides contribute
You’re in a neuroimaging/psychology context

title: Lesson 3: Types of PLS Methods
text:
Neuroimaging PLS Variants
In neuroimaging, PLS-C is further specialized based on the design matrix (Y):

Mean-Centered PLS (Task PLS)
The simplest form. Y is a design matrix indicating group/condition membership.


Code
# Example: 2 conditions, 3 subjects each
n_per_cond <- 15
n_cond <- 2
n <- n_per_cond * n_cond

# Design matrix (dummy coded)
Y_design <- matrix(0, n, n_cond)
Y_design[1:n_per_cond, 1] <- 1
Y_design[(n_per_cond+1):n, 2] <- 1

# Visualize
design_df <- data.frame(
  Subject = 1:n,
  Condition = rep(c("A", "B"), each = n_per_cond)
)

p1 <- ggplot(design_df, aes(x = factor(Subject), y = 1, fill = Condition)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", height = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("A" = "#4575b4", "B" = "#d73027")) +
  labs(title = "Design Matrix Y",
       subtitle = "Subjects in two conditions",
       x = "Subject", y = "") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())

# What Mean-Centered PLS finds
cat("Mean-Centered PLS asks:\n")


Mean-Centered PLS asks:


Code
cat("Which brain regions differ between conditions?\n\n")


Which brain regions differ between conditions?


Code
print(p1)









Use when: Comparing groups or conditions


Behavior PLS
Y contains continuous behavioral measures for each subject.


Code
# Example: 3 behavioral measures
n <- 30
Y_behav <- data.frame(
  Subject = 1:n,
  Memory = rnorm(n, 100, 15),
  Attention = rnorm(n, 50, 10),
  Speed = rnorm(n, 200, 30)
)

# Visualize
library(tidyr)
Y_long <- pivot_longer(Y_behav, cols = -Subject, names_to = "Measure", values_to = "Score")

ggplot(Y_long, aes(x = factor(Subject), y = Score, fill = Measure)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Behavior Matrix Y",
       subtitle = "Continuous behavioral measures per subject",
       x = "Subject") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7))









Use when: Relating brain patterns to continuous behavioral measures


Task PLS
Combines both: Subjects have multiple conditions, and the analysis finds patterns that differ across conditions.


Code
# Task PLS structure:
# Rows = subjects × conditions (stacked)
# Y = condition indicators

n_subj <- 10
n_cond <- 3

cat("Task PLS Data Structure:\n")


Task PLS Data Structure:


Code
cat("========================\n")


========================


Code
cat("Brain data (X): ", n_subj * n_cond, "rows (", n_subj, "subjects ×",
    n_cond, "conditions)\n")


Brain data (X):  30 rows ( 10 subjects × 3 conditions)


Code
cat("Design matrix (Y):", n_cond, "columns (condition indicators)\n")


Design matrix (Y): 3 columns (condition indicators)


Code
cat("\nFinds: Brain patterns that characterize each condition\n")



Finds: Brain patterns that characterize each condition

title: Lesson 3: Types of PLS Methods
text:
Key Takeaways






TipRemember




PLS-R is for prediction; PLS-C is for pattern discovery
Within PLS-C, the variant depends on what Y contains
Mean-Centered PLS: Compare groups/conditions
Behavior PLS: Relate brain to continuous measures
Task PLS: Characterize conditions with repeated measures
The core math (SVD on cross-product) is the same - the input differs!

title: Lesson 1: Why Multivariate Analysis?
text:
By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

Why simple correlations fail with many variables
The concept of latent variables (hidden patterns)
The difference between correlation and covariance
What it means to find optimal weighted combinations

title: Lesson 1: Why Multivariate Analysis?
text:
The Problem with Many Variables

A Simple Example First
Imagine you measure two things on 50 students:

Hours studied
Exam score

Finding the relationship is easy: compute the correlation.


Code
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)

# Simple two-variable case
n <- 50
hours <- runif(n, 1, 10)
score <- 50 + 4 * hours + rnorm(n, sd = 8)

df <- data.frame(hours = hours, score = score)

ggplot(df, aes(x = hours, y = score)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Simple Relationship",
       subtitle = sprintf("r = %.2f", cor(hours, score)),
       x = "Hours Studied", y = "Exam Score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)









One correlation. One relationship. Easy.


Now Make It Harder
But what if you measure:

10 study behaviors: hours, breaks, note-taking, practice tests, etc.
8 outcomes: multiple exam scores, project grades, participation, etc.

Now you have 10 × 8 = 80 correlations to examine!


Code
set.seed(42)

# Simulate multiple variables
n <- 50
p1 <- 10  # Study behaviors
p2 <- 8   # Outcomes

X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p1), n, p1)
Y <- matrix(rnorm(n * p2), n, p2)

# Add some real relationships
Y[, 1:3] <- Y[, 1:3] + 0.5 * X[, 1:3]  # Some behaviors predict some outcomes

# Compute all correlations
cor_matrix <- cor(X, Y)

# Visualize
cor_df <- expand.grid(
  StudyBehavior = paste0("Behavior", 1:p1),
  Outcome = paste0("Outcome", 1:p2)
)
cor_df$correlation <- as.vector(cor_matrix)

ggplot(cor_df, aes(x = Outcome, y = StudyBehavior, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", correlation)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#4575b4", mid = "white", high = "#d73027",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "80 Correlations to Examine",
       subtitle = "Which ones matter? Is there a pattern?") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))











The Problems Multiply
With 80 correlations:

Multiple testing: By chance, some will be “significant” even if nothing is real
Redundancy: Many variables measure similar things
No big picture: Hard to see if there’s an underlying pattern
Overfitting: Easy to find spurious relationships







ImportantThe Core Problem



We don’t want 80 separate relationships. We want to know:
Is there a pattern of study behaviors that relates to a pattern of outcomes?

title: Lesson 1: Why Multivariate Analysis?
text:
The Idea of Latent Variables

What is a Latent Variable?
A latent variable is a hidden factor that you don’t measure directly but that influences the things you do measure.
Example: You don’t measure “intelligence” directly. Instead, you measure: - Vocabulary test score - Math test score - Pattern recognition score
“Intelligence” is a latent variable that influences all three observed scores.











PLS Finds Latent Variables in TWO Sets
PLS goes further. It finds latent variables that:

Explain variation within each variable set
Are maximally related to each other between sets

title: Lesson 1: Why Multivariate Analysis?
text:
Correlation vs Covariance

Why Does This Matter?
PLS can maximize either correlation or covariance between latent variables. Understanding the difference is crucial.


Correlation
Correlation measures the strength of a linear relationship, ignoring scale.

Ranges from -1 to +1
Unaffected by units (inches vs centimeters)
Height in inches vs height in cm have r = 1.0

\[r = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\text{SD}(X) \times \text{SD}(Y)}\]


Covariance
Covariance measures how variables move together, considering their scales.

Can be any value (positive or negative)
Larger when variables have more variance
Affected by units

\[\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})\]


Visual Comparison


Code
set.seed(42)
library(patchwork)

# Same correlation, different covariances
n <- 100

# Small variance
x1 <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)
y1 <- 0.7 * x1 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7)

# Large variance (same correlation!)
x2 <- rnorm(n, 0, 5)
y2 <- 0.7 * x2 + rnorm(n, 0, 3.5)

p1 <- ggplot(data.frame(x = x1, y = y1), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
  xlim(-15, 15) + ylim(-15, 15) +
  labs(title = "Small Variance",
       subtitle = sprintf("r = %.2f, Cov = %.2f", cor(x1, y1), cov(x1, y1))) +
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_fixed()

p2 <- ggplot(data.frame(x = x2, y = y2), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
  xlim(-15, 15) + ylim(-15, 15) +
  labs(title = "Large Variance",
       subtitle = sprintf("r = %.2f, Cov = %.2f", cor(x2, y2), cov(x2, y2))) +
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_fixed()

p1 + p2 + plot_annotation(
  title = "Same Correlation, Different Covariance",
  subtitle = "Covariance captures both relationship strength AND variance"
)















NotePLS and Covariance



Standard PLS maximizes covariance, which means it finds patterns that:

Have strong relationships (high correlation)
Explain substantial variance in the data

This often gives more interpretable results than maximizing correlation alone.

title: Lesson 1: Why Multivariate Analysis?
text:
Weighted Combinations

What is a Weighted Combination?
Instead of looking at variables individually, we combine them:
\[\text{Score} = w_1 \times \text{Var}_1 + w_2 \times \text{Var}_2 + w_3 \times \text{Var}_3 + ...\]
The weights (w) determine how much each variable contributes.


A Concrete Example
Suppose you measure study behaviors:



Student
Hours
Practice Tests
Notes Pages




A
5
3
10


B
8
5
15


C
3
1
5



A weighted “study intensity” score might be:
\[\text{Study Intensity} = 0.4 \times \text{Hours} + 0.5 \times \text{Practice} + 0.1 \times \text{Notes}\]
For Student A: 0.4(5) + 0.5(3) + 0.1(10) = 2.0 + 1.5 + 1.0 = 4.5


Why Weights Matter
Different weights emphasize different aspects:


Code
# Example with different weights
students <- data.frame(
  Student = LETTERS[1:10],
  Hours = c(5, 8, 3, 7, 6, 4, 9, 2, 6, 5),
  Practice = c(3, 5, 1, 4, 3, 2, 6, 1, 4, 3),
  Notes = c(10, 15, 5, 8, 12, 20, 10, 3, 8, 15)
)

# Two different weighting schemes
students$Score_Hours <- with(students, 0.8 * Hours + 0.1 * Practice + 0.1 * Notes)
students$Score_Balanced <- with(students, 0.33 * Hours + 0.33 * Practice + 0.33 * Notes)

# Compare
library(tidyr)
scores_long <- pivot_longer(students,
                             cols = c(Score_Hours, Score_Balanced),
                             names_to = "Weighting",
                             values_to = "Score")
scores_long$Weighting <- ifelse(scores_long$Weighting == "Score_Hours",
                                 "Heavy on Hours (0.8, 0.1, 0.1)",
                                 "Balanced (0.33, 0.33, 0.33)")

ggplot(scores_long, aes(x = Student, y = Score, fill = Weighting)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#4575b4", "#d73027")) +
  labs(title = "Same Data, Different Weights = Different Scores",
       subtitle = "PLS finds the weights that maximize covariance with the other variable set",
       y = "Weighted Score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)











PLS Finds Optimal Weights
The key insight: PLS finds the weights that create scores with maximum covariance between the two variable sets.
You don’t choose the weights - the algorithm discovers them from the data!

title: Lesson 1: Why Multivariate Analysis?
text:
Putting It All Together

What PLS Does (Conceptually)

Takes two variable sets (e.g., brain and behavior)
Finds weights for each variable in each set
Creates latent variables (weighted combinations)
Optimizes so the latent variables have maximum covariance
Repeats to find additional, orthogonal patterns



Visual Summary

title: Lesson 1: Why Multivariate Analysis?
text:
Key Takeaways






TipSummary




The problem: Many variables create too many correlations to interpret
The solution: Find weighted combinations (latent variables) that capture the essential relationships
PLS approach: Maximize covariance between latent variables from two different datasets
Why covariance: It balances relationship strength with variance explained
The weights: These tell you which original variables matter most for the pattern

title: Lesson 1: Why Multivariate Analysis?
text:

You’ll learn: - The mathematical machinery behind PLS - What “singular values” represent - How multiple latent variables are found - Why PLS is computationally efficient

title: Lesson 2: The PLS Algorithm
text:
By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

How PLS uses the cross-covariance matrix
What Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) does

title: Lesson 2: The PLS Algorithm
text:
The Cross-Covariance Matrix

Starting Point: Two Data Matrices
We have:

X: Brain data (n subjects × p brain variables)
Y: Behavior data (n subjects × q behavior variables)

Both matrices have the same subjects in rows.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
set.seed(42)

# Create example data
n <- 30  # subjects
p <- 5   # brain variables
q <- 3   # behavior variables

# Generate data with a real relationship
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
colnames(X) <- paste0("Brain", 1:p)

# Y is related to X through a latent pattern
latent <- X[, 1] - X[, 2]  # True latent variable
Y <- matrix(rnorm(n * q), n, q)
Y[, 1] <- Y[, 1] + 0.8 * latent  # Behavior 1 related to latent
Y[, 2] <- Y[, 2] + 0.5 * latent  # Behavior 2 somewhat related
colnames(Y) <- paste0("Behav", 1:q)

cat("X dimensions:", dim(X), "(subjects × brain variables)\n")


X dimensions: 30 5 (subjects × brain variables)


Code
cat("Y dimensions:", dim(Y), "(subjects × behavior variables)\n")


Y dimensions: 30 3 (subjects × behavior variables)




Building the Cross-Covariance Matrix
The cross-covariance matrix R captures all pairwise covariances between X and Y variables:
\[R = X^T Y\]
(After mean-centering both X and Y)


Code
# Mean-center the data
X_centered <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
Y_centered <- scale(Y, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)

# Compute cross-covariance matrix
R <- t(X_centered) %*% Y_centered / (n - 1)

cat("Cross-covariance matrix R dimensions:", dim(R), "\n")


Cross-covariance matrix R dimensions: 5 3 


Code
cat("(brain variables × behavior variables)\n\n")


(brain variables × behavior variables)


Code
# Visualize
R_df <- expand.grid(
  Brain = colnames(X),
  Behavior = colnames(Y)
)
R_df$Covariance <- as.vector(R)

ggplot(R_df, aes(x = Behavior, y = Brain, fill = Covariance)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Covariance)), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#4575b4", mid = "white", high = "#d73027",
                       midpoint = 0) +
  labs(title = "Cross-Covariance Matrix R",
       subtitle = "Each cell shows how one brain variable covaries with one behavior") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)











What R Tells Us

Each entry R[i,j] = covariance between brain variable i and behavior variable j
Positive values: variables tend to increase together
Negative values: one increases as the other decreases
Near zero: little linear relationship







NoteThe Problem



R has p × q entries (5 × 3 = 15 in our example). We want to find the single best pattern that captures the most important relationship.

title: Lesson 2: The PLS Algorithm
text:
Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

The Magic Tool
SVD is a mathematical technique that decomposes any matrix into three parts:
\[R = U \cdot S \cdot V^T\]
Where:

U: Left singular vectors (weights for X variables) - called “brain saliences”
S: Singular values (diagonal matrix of pattern strengths)
V: Right singular vectors (weights for Y variables) - called “behavior saliences”



Code
# Perform SVD on the cross-covariance matrix
svd_result <- svd(R)

# Extract components
U <- svd_result$u  # Brain saliences
S <- svd_result$d  # Singular values
V <- svd_result$v  # Behavior saliences

cat("U (brain saliences):", dim(U), "\n")


U (brain saliences): 5 3 


Code
cat("S (singular values):", length(S), "values\n")


S (singular values): 3 values


Code
cat("V (behavior saliences):", dim(V), "\n")


V (behavior saliences): 3 3 




Visualizing SVD Components


Code
# Create visualization of the first latent variable
lv1_brain <- data.frame(
  Variable = colnames(X),
  Salience = U[, 1]
)

lv1_behav <- data.frame(
  Variable = colnames(Y),
  Salience = V[, 1]
)

p1 <- ggplot(lv1_brain, aes(x = Variable, y = Salience, fill = Salience > 0)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#4575b4", "TRUE" = "#d73027"),
                    guide = "none") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Brain Saliences (U)",
       subtitle = "LV1: How each brain variable contributes",
       y = "Weight") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  coord_flip()

p2 <- ggplot(lv1_behav, aes(x = Variable, y = Salience, fill = Salience > 0)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#4575b4", "TRUE" = "#d73027"),
                    guide = "none") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Behavior Saliences (V)",
       subtitle = "LV1: How each behavior contributes",
       y = "Weight") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  coord_flip()

p1 + p2 + plot_annotation(
  title = sprintf("First Latent Variable (Singular Value = %.2f)", S[1])
)











Understanding Saliences (Weights)
Saliences tell you how much each original variable contributes to the pattern:

Large positive: Variable strongly contributes in the positive direction
Large negative: Variable strongly contributes in the negative direction
Near zero: Variable doesn’t contribute much to this pattern

In our example:


Code
cat("Brain saliences for LV1:\n")


Brain saliences for LV1:


Code
for (i in 1:p) {
  cat(sprintf("  %s: %.3f %s\n", colnames(X)[i], U[i, 1],
              ifelse(abs(U[i, 1]) > 0.3, "(important)", "")))
}


  Brain1: -0.834 (important)
  Brain2: 0.542 (important)
  Brain3: 0.029 
  Brain4: 0.083 
  Brain5: 0.061 


Code
cat("\nBehavior saliences for LV1:\n")



Behavior saliences for LV1:


Code
for (i in 1:q) {
  cat(sprintf("  %s: %.3f %s\n", colnames(Y)[i], V[i, 1],
              ifelse(abs(V[i, 1]) > 0.3, "(important)", "")))
}


  Behav1: -0.887 (important)
  Behav2: -0.461 (important)
  Behav3: -0.025

title: Lesson 2: The PLS Algorithm
text:
Computing Scores

What Are Scores?
Scores represent how strongly each subject expresses the pattern:

Brain scores: X multiplied by brain saliences
Behavior scores: Y multiplied by behavior saliences



Code
# Compute scores
brain_scores <- X_centered %*% U[, 1]
behavior_scores <- Y_centered %*% V[, 1]

# Show first few subjects
cat("First 5 subjects' scores:\n")


First 5 subjects' scores:


Code
score_df <- data.frame(
  Subject = 1:5,
  Brain_Score = round(brain_scores[1:5], 3),
  Behavior_Score = round(behavior_scores[1:5], 3)
)
print(score_df)


  Subject Brain_Score Behavior_Score
1       1      -0.748         -0.765
2       2       0.865          2.887
3       3       0.471         -0.477
4       4      -0.627         -0.960
5       5      -0.042          0.725




The Beautiful Relationship
The correlation between brain scores and behavior scores equals the singular value (when properly normalized):


Code
# Create scatter plot
score_data <- data.frame(
  Brain = brain_scores,
  Behavior = behavior_scores
)

r_value <- cor(brain_scores, behavior_scores)

ggplot(score_data, aes(x = Brain, y = Behavior)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7, color = "#4575b4") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#d73027") +
  labs(title = "Brain Scores vs Behavior Scores",
       subtitle = sprintf("Correlation r = %.3f", r_value),
       x = "Brain Score (LV1)",
       y = "Behavior Score (LV1)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)















ImportantKey Insight



The singular value represents the strength of the relationship captured by each latent variable.

Larger singular value = stronger brain-behavior relationship
First LV has the largest singular value (most important pattern)
Subsequent LVs capture remaining patterns in decreasing order

title: Lesson 2: The PLS Algorithm
text:
Multiple Latent Variables

Why Multiple?
One pattern rarely tells the whole story. SVD finds all possible orthogonal patterns, ordered by importance.


Code
# Singular values show importance of each LV
sv_df <- data.frame(
  LV = 1:length(S),
  Singular_Value = S,
  Variance_Pct = (S^2) / sum(S^2) * 100
)

p1 <- ggplot(sv_df, aes(x = factor(LV), y = Singular_Value)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "#4575b4", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Singular Values",
       subtitle = "Strength of each pattern",
       x = "Latent Variable", y = "Singular Value") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p2 <- ggplot(sv_df, aes(x = factor(LV), y = Variance_Pct)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "#d73027", color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", Variance_Pct)), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Variance Explained",
       subtitle = "Relative importance",
       x = "Latent Variable", y = "% of Total") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p1 + p2











Orthogonality
Each subsequent LV is orthogonal (uncorrelated) to previous ones:


Code
# Compute all brain scores
all_brain_scores <- X_centered %*% U

# Check correlations between LV scores
cat("Correlations between brain scores of different LVs:\n")


Correlations between brain scores of different LVs:


Code
cor_matrix <- cor(all_brain_scores)
print(round(cor_matrix, 4))


        [,1]    [,2]   [,3]
[1,]  1.0000 -0.1285 0.0546
[2,] -0.1285  1.0000 0.0772
[3,]  0.0546  0.0772 1.0000


This means each LV captures a unique pattern not explained by others.

title: Lesson 2: The PLS Algorithm
text:
The Complete PLS Process

Step-by-Step Summary











In Code


Code
# Complete PLS implementation
pls_simple <- function(X, Y) {
  # Step 1-2: Mean center
  X_c <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
  Y_c <- scale(Y, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)

  # Step 3: Cross-covariance matrix
  n <- nrow(X)
  R <- t(X_c) %*% Y_c / (n - 1)

  # Step 4: SVD
  svd_result <- svd(R)

  # Step 5: Compute scores
  brain_scores <- X_c %*% svd_result$u
  behavior_scores <- Y_c %*% svd_result$v

  list(
    u = svd_result$u,           # Brain saliences
    v = svd_result$v,           # Behavior saliences
    s = svd_result$d,           # Singular values
    brain_scores = brain_scores,
    behavior_scores = behavior_scores
  )
}

# Run it
result <- pls_simple(X, Y)

cat("PLS Results:\n")


PLS Results:


Code
cat("Singular values:", round(result$s, 3), "\n")


Singular values: 2.026 0.423 0.198 


Code
cat("Variance explained:", round((result$s^2)/sum(result$s^2)*100, 1), "%\n")


Variance explained: 95 4.1 0.9 %

title: Lesson 2: The PLS Algorithm
text:
What Makes PLS Special?

The Optimization Problem
PLS solves:
\[\max_{u, v} \text{Cov}(Xu, Yv)\]
Subject to: \(||u|| = 1\) and \(||v|| = 1\)
In words: Find unit-length weight vectors that maximize the covariance of the resulting scores.


Why SVD Solves This
Mathematical fact: The first left/right singular vectors of R are exactly the weight vectors that maximize this covariance!
This is why PLS is so elegant - a complex optimization problem has a simple, efficient solution.

title: Lesson 2: The PLS Algorithm
text:
Key Terminology Summary



Term
Symbol
Meaning




Saliences
U, V
Weights for original variables


Singular values
S
Strength of each LV pattern


Scores
XU, YV
Subject-level expression of pattern


Latent variable
LV
The weighted combination/pattern


Cross-covariance
R
Matrix of all X-Y covariances

title: Lesson 2: The PLS Algorithm
text:
Hands-On Exercise
Try modifying the strength of the brain-behavior relationship:


Code
# Create data with stronger relationship
set.seed(123)
n <- 50
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 5), n, 5)
latent <- X[, 1] + X[, 2]  # Latent pattern in brain

# Change this multiplier to see effect on singular values
strength <- 1.0  # Try 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0

Y <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n, 3)
Y[, 1] <- Y[, 1] + strength * latent

result <- pls_simple(X, Y)
cat("Strength:", strength, "-> First singular value:", round(result$s[1], 3), "\n")

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

title: Lesson 4: PLS vs CCA and Related Methods
text:
The Method Landscape
Several methods relate two sets of variables. Understanding their differences helps you choose wisely.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(MASS)  # For CCA via cancor
set.seed(42)

# Create common dataset for all comparisons
n <- 100
p <- 8   # X variables
q <- 4   # Y variables

# Generate correlated data
Sigma <- matrix(0.3, p + q, p + q)
diag(Sigma) <- 1
# Make X and Y blocks more correlated internally
Sigma[1:p, 1:p] <- 0.4
diag(Sigma[1:p, 1:p]) <- 1
Sigma[(p+1):(p+q), (p+1):(p+q)] <- 0.4
diag(Sigma[(p+1):(p+q), (p+1):(p+q)]) <- 1
# Create cross-correlation
Sigma[1:3, (p+1):(p+2)] <- 0.5
Sigma[(p+1):(p+2), 1:3] <- 0.5

data <- mvrnorm(n, rep(0, p + q), Sigma)
X <- data[, 1:p]
Y <- data[, (p+1):(p+q)]
colnames(X) <- paste0("X", 1:p)
colnames(Y) <- paste0("Y", 1:q)

title: Lesson 4: PLS vs CCA and Related Methods
text:
Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA)

What CCA Does
CCA finds linear combinations of X and Y that have maximum correlation (not covariance).
\[\max_{a, b} \text{Corr}(Xa, Yb)\]
Subject to the combinations having unit variance.


CCA Algorithm


Code
# Perform CCA using cancor()
cca_result <- cancor(X, Y)

cat("CCA Results:\n")


CCA Results:


Code
cat("============\n")


============


Code
cat("Canonical correlations:", round(cca_result$cor, 3), "\n")


Canonical correlations: 0.834 0.48 0.304 0.15 


Code
# First canonical variates
a1 <- cca_result$xcoef[, 1]
b1 <- cca_result$ycoef[, 1]

# Compute canonical variates
X_c <- scale(X)
Y_c <- scale(Y)
xi_1 <- X_c %*% a1
eta_1 <- Y_c %*% b1

cat("\nFirst pair correlation:", round(cor(xi_1, eta_1), 3), "\n")



First pair correlation: 0.834 




Visualizing CCA


Code
# Compare first canonical variates
cca_df <- data.frame(
  X_canonical = xi_1,
  Y_canonical = eta_1
)

p1 <- ggplot(cca_df, aes(x = X_canonical, y = Y_canonical)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 3, color = "#4575b4") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#d73027") +
  labs(title = "CCA: First Canonical Variates",
       subtitle = sprintf("Canonical correlation = %.3f", cca_result$cor[1]),
       x = "X Canonical Variate 1",
       y = "Y Canonical Variate 1") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# CCA coefficients
coef_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = c(colnames(X), colnames(Y)),
  Coefficient = c(a1, b1),
  Set = rep(c("X", "Y"), c(p, q))
)

p2 <- ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = Variable, y = Coefficient, fill = Set)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("X" = "#4575b4", "Y" = "#d73027")) +
  labs(title = "CCA Coefficients",
       subtitle = "Weights for first canonical variates") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  coord_flip()

p1 + p2











The Key Difference: Correlation vs Covariance


Code
# PLS (covariance)
X_centered <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
Y_centered <- scale(Y, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
R_cov <- t(X_centered) %*% Y_centered / (n - 1)
svd_pls <- svd(R_cov)

# PLS scores
pls_brain <- X_centered %*% svd_pls$u[, 1]
pls_behav <- Y_centered %*% svd_pls$v[, 1]

# Compare
comp_df <- data.frame(
  CCA_X = scale(xi_1),
  CCA_Y = scale(eta_1),
  PLS_X = scale(pls_brain),
  PLS_Y = scale(pls_behav)
)

p1 <- ggplot(comp_df, aes(x = CCA_X, y = CCA_Y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "#4575b4") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs(title = "CCA",
       subtitle = sprintf("Maximizes correlation\nr = %.3f", cor(xi_1, eta_1)),
       x = "X score", y = "Y score") +
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_fixed()

p2 <- ggplot(comp_df, aes(x = PLS_X, y = PLS_Y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "#d73027") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs(title = "PLS",
       subtitle = sprintf("Maximizes covariance\nr = %.3f, cov = %.2f",
                          cor(pls_brain, pls_behav),
                          cov(pls_brain, pls_behav)),
       x = "X score", y = "Y score") +
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_fixed()

p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(title = "CCA vs PLS: Same Data, Different Objectives")











CCA Strengths and Limitations






TipCCA Strengths




Finds maximum correlation between variable sets
Scale-invariant: unaffected by variable units
Well-established statistical properties
Clear interpretation as correlation









WarningCCA Limitations




Requires n > p + q: Needs more observations than total variables
Sensitive to multicollinearity: Unstable when variables are highly correlated
Ignores variance: May find correlations in low-variance directions
Can be unreliable with high-dimensional data

title: Lesson 4: PLS vs CCA and Related Methods
section: PLS vs CCA: When Does It Matter?
text:
PLS vs CCA: When Does It Matter?

Sample Size Requirements


Code
# Demonstrate CCA failure with p > n
set.seed(123)
n_small <- 20
p_big <- 30

X_big <- matrix(rnorm(n_small * p_big), n_small, p_big)
Y_small <- matrix(rnorm(n_small * 3), n_small, 3)

# CCA will have issues
cat("Sample size:", n_small, "\n")


Sample size: 20 


Code
cat("X variables:", p_big, "\n")


X variables: 30 


Code
cat("Total variables:", p_big + 3, "\n")


Total variables: 33 


Code
cat("CCA requires n >", p_big + 3, "but we have n =", n_small, "\n\n")


CCA requires n > 33 but we have n = 20 


Code
# Try CCA (will give fewer canonical correlations)
cca_small <- cancor(X_big, Y_small)
cat("CCA canonical correlations:", length(cca_small$cor), "\n")


CCA canonical correlations: 3 


Code

(Limited to min(n-1, p, q) = 3 )


Code
# PLS works fine
X_c <- scale(X_big, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
Y_c <- scale(Y_small, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
R <- t(X_c) %*% Y_c
svd_r <- svd(R)
cat("PLS singular values:", round(svd_r$d[1:3], 3), "\n")


PLS singular values: 28.797 23.254 16.81 


Code
cat("PLS works regardless of p vs n!\n")


PLS works regardless of p vs n!




High-Dimensional Visualization

title: Lesson 4: PLS vs CCA and Related Methods
text:
Principal Component Regression (PCR)

What PCR Does
PCR is a two-step process:

Perform PCA on X to get components
Regress Y on the PCA components












PCR Implementation


Code
# PCR implementation
# Step 1: PCA on X
pca_X <- prcomp(X, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

# Step 2: Regress Y on first k components
k <- 3  # Number of components
pc_scores <- pca_X$x[, 1:k]

# Regression
pcr_model <- lm(Y[, 1] ~ pc_scores)

cat("PCR Results (predicting Y1):\n")


PCR Results (predicting Y1):


Code
cat("============================\n")


============================


Code
cat("Variance explained by first", k, "PCs:",
    round(sum(pca_X$sdev[1:k]^2) / sum(pca_X$sdev^2) * 100, 1), "%\n")


Variance explained by first 3 PCs: 67.9 %


Code
cat("R² of regression:", round(summary(pcr_model)$r.squared, 3), "\n")


R² of regression: 0.359 




The PCR Problem
PCR finds directions that explain variance in X, not relationships with Y.


Code
# Create extreme example
set.seed(456)
n <- 100

# X1 has high variance but no relation to Y
# X2 has low variance but strong relation to Y
X_demo <- cbind(
  X1 = rnorm(n, sd = 10),  # High variance, unrelated
  X2 = rnorm(n, sd = 1)    # Low variance
)
Y_demo <- 2 * X_demo[, 2] + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)  # Y depends on X2!

# PCA picks X1 first
pca_demo <- prcomp(X_demo, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)

# PCR with 1 component (will use mostly X1)
pc1 <- pca_demo$x[, 1]
pcr_r2 <- cor(pc1, Y_demo)^2

# Compare to using X2 directly
direct_r2 <- cor(X_demo[, 2], Y_demo)^2

cat("PCA loadings (PC1):\n")


PCA loadings (PC1):


Code
cat("  X1:", round(pca_demo$rotation[1, 1], 3), "(high variance variable)\n")


  X1: 1 (high variance variable)


Code
cat("  X2:", round(pca_demo$rotation[2, 1], 3), "(predictive variable)\n\n")


  X2: -0.002 (predictive variable)


Code
cat("R² predicting Y:\n")


R² predicting Y:


Code
cat("  Using PC1 (PCR):", round(pcr_r2, 3), "\n")


  Using PC1 (PCR): 0 


Code
cat("  Using X2 directly:", round(direct_r2, 3), "\n\n")


  Using X2 directly: 0.944 


Code
cat("PCR misses the relationship because PCA ignores Y!\n")


PCR misses the relationship because PCA ignores Y!




PCR vs PLS Comparison


Code
# Using our demonstration data
# PLS would find X2
X_c <- scale(X_demo, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
Y_c <- scale(Y_demo, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
R <- t(X_c) %*% Y_c
svd_pls <- svd(R)

pls_weights <- svd_pls$u[, 1]
pls_score <- X_c %*% pls_weights
pls_r2 <- cor(pls_score, Y_demo)^2

cat("Method comparison:\n")


Method comparison:


Code
cat("==================\n")


==================


Code
cat("PCR weight on X1:", round(pca_demo$rotation[1, 1], 3), "\n")


PCR weight on X1: 1 


Code
cat("PCR weight on X2:", round(pca_demo$rotation[2, 1], 3), "\n")


PCR weight on X2: -0.002 


Code
cat("PCR R² with Y:", round(pcr_r2, 3), "\n\n")


PCR R² with Y: 0 


Code
cat("PLS weight on X1:", round(pls_weights[1], 3), "\n")


PLS weight on X1: 0.141 


Code
cat("PLS weight on X2:", round(pls_weights[2], 3), "\n")


PLS weight on X2: 0.99 


Code
cat("PLS R² with Y:", round(pls_r2, 3), "\n")


PLS R² with Y: 0.317 








ImportantKey Insight



PLS beats PCR when the directions of maximum variance in X are not the most predictive of Y. PLS explicitly looks for X directions that relate to Y.

title: Lesson 4: PLS vs CCA and Related Methods
text:
Reduced Rank Regression (RRR)

What RRR Does
RRR finds the best low-rank approximation to the regression coefficient matrix:
\[Y = XB + E, \quad \text{where } B \text{ has rank } k\]
It’s a compromise between full regression and PCA-style dimension reduction.


Relationship to PLS
RRR can be viewed as finding the same subspace as PLS, but:

RRR minimizes prediction error
PLS maximizes covariance

For standardized data, they often give similar results.

title: Lesson 4: PLS vs CCA and Related Methods
text:
Key Takeaways






TipSummary




CCA maximizes correlation; needs n > p + q; scale-invariant
PLS maximizes covariance; works with any n, p; accounts for variance
PCR ignores Y when finding X components; can miss predictive patterns
Use CCA when you have enough samples and want correlation focus
Use PLS for high-dimensional data or when variance matters
PLS is more robust to the common problems in neuroimaging data
